155.title: Beads and silence
155.hook: Catholics pray the rosary and keep adoration before the sacrament; the Catholic path goes deeper
155.tomorrow: camp 3 close: a rule of life
155.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the rosary daily or weekly, alone or in groups, and some keep an hour of silent adoration before the Eucharist; Orthodox Christians often pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope, and some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: confession and anointing, honest words and healing oil. Your line was said out loud, it loosens. Did something loosen? Day one hundred fifty-five.

Watch an elderly woman in the back pew of a Catholic church on a weekday afternoon. The church is nearly empty. Her lips are moving, barely. And in her hands, a loop of small beads slides, one at a time, through her fingers. She isn't reading. She's not looking at anything in particular. Her fingers know the way, the way your fingers know a zipper or a phone code. Maybe she's praying for a grandson. Maybe she's just resting. Many Catholics have seen a grandmother do this. Some have seen a rosary tucked into a coffin, or hanging from a rearview mirror. Today's word is that loop of beads, and what it does with a restless pair of hands.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHURCH, A WEEKDAY.` → `BEADS SLIDING THROUGH HER FINGERS.` → `HER HANDS KNOW THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Rosary. From the Latin rosarium, a rose garden: a garland of prayers. The rosary is a string of beads grouped in tens, called decades. On each large bead, a person prays the Our Father. On each of the ten small beads, a Hail Mary. Then a short prayer of praise, Glory be to the Father. Five decades make a usual rosary. The Hail Mary begins with the angel's greeting to Mary in Luke's gospel, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." It goes on with words from her cousin Elizabeth and a request for Mary's prayers. But the words are only half of it. While the lips repeat, the mind walks slowly through scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries: the joyful ones, like the birth in Bethlehem; the sorrowful ones, like the cross; the glorious ones, like the resurrection. In 2002, Pope John Paul the Second added a fourth set, the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. The repetition isn't meant to be boring. It's like waves: the words settle the body so the heart can look. Then there's the silence. Many Catholics keep adoration: sitting quietly in a chapel before the consecrated bread of the Eucharist, displayed on the altar, sometimes for an hour, sometimes through the night, taking turns. No words needed. Orthodox Christians use a knotted prayer rope with the Jesus Prayer. Some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too. Most Protestants don't pray the rosary, because they don't address prayers to Mary, and many pray without beads at all. For the Catholics who use them, the beads keep the hands busy so the heart can be still. The Catholic path on Infinite Hill goes much deeper into both.
screen: `ROSARIUM — A GARLAND OF ROSES.` · `DECADES: ONE OUR FATHER, TEN HAIL MARYS.` · `THE LIPS REPEAT, THE HEART LOOKS.` · `ADORATION: SILENCE BEFORE THE SACRAMENT.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Find something small to hold. A rosary or prayer rope if you have one. If not, a smooth stone, a ring, a button, even your own fingers, one at a time. Let your hand hold it and move slowly. With each small movement, one breath. If you pray, you can let each breath carry a short prayer you already know, or just a name. If you don't, let the object anchor you here. Notice how busy hands can quiet a busy head. The bell holds the time.
Rosary. Latin for a rose garden: a loop of beads, decades of prayer, and scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
Your line: the hands can pray too. Today, hold something in your hand while you pray or sit still for a minute. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
156.hook: monks and Methodists alike write a simple rule: what I'll do daily, weekly, yearly
156.howItsDone: Monks and nuns live by a written rule such as the Rule of Saint Benedict, early Methodists kept Wesley's General Rules, and many Christians today write a short personal rule of daily, weekly and yearly practices, often with a spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rosary, beads for the hands and silence for the heart. Your line was the hands can pray too. What did you hold? Today is the last day of camp three. Day one hundred fifty-six.
screen: `THE HANDS CAN PRAY TOO.` → `THE LAST DAY OF CAMP THREE.`

segments.voice: This camp started with a simple question: what is prayer? Since then you've met a lot of practices. The Jesus Prayer and the psalter. Lectio divina and the examen. Lament and the icon. Advent, Lent and Pascha. The sabbath. The canon and translation. The tithe, alms and hospitality. The hymn and the spiritual. Koinonia, fasting and testimony. The sacraments and the rosary. That's a lot. Nobody does all of them, and nobody is meant to. So how do Christians actually choose? One old answer is a short written plan. Monks have one. Methodists have one. Today's word is the thing that holds the practices together.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS OF PRACTICES.` → `NOBODY DOES ALL OF THEM.` → `A SHORT WRITTEN PLAN.`

segments.voice: Rule of life. The word rule comes from the Latin regula, which first meant a straight stick, a ruler, something to keep a line from wandering. A rule of life isn't a list of prohibitions. It's a simple, honest plan for what you'll actually do: daily, weekly, yearly. Take the Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks in Italy. It covers prayer, work, meals, sleep, guests, even how much wine is allowed. And near its end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners. Monks and nuns still live by that little rule. A popular motto, pray and work, is often pinned on Benedict, though it doesn't appear in the rule itself. It does sum up its rhythm. Much later, John Wesley wrote the General Rules for the Methodists, and they fit on a page: do no harm, do good, and keep the practices of the church, like prayer, scripture, the Lord's Supper and fasting. Short enough to remember. Today many Christians, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and evangelical, write their own short rule. Something like: daily, ten minutes of prayer and a psalm. Weekly, church and a sabbath afternoon. Monthly, a fast day. Yearly, a retreat. The secret of a good rule is that it's small enough to keep. A rule you'll really follow beats a grand one you'll abandon by Thursday. A trellis in a garden doesn't make the vine grow. It gives it something to climb. That's today's line: small rules keep big loves. And tomorrow, camp four begins: the text itself, read in order, starting with the Gospel of Mark.
screen: `REGULA — A STRAIGHT STICK.` · `BENEDICT: A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · `WESLEY: NO HARM, DO GOOD, PRACTICE.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO KEEP.` · then, large: `SMALL RULES KEEP BIG LOVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Get a pen, or your notes. Breathe. Look back over this camp and ask which one or two practices actually stuck, or quietly called to you. Now write three lines. Daily: one small thing, five minutes or less. Weekly: one thing. Yearly: one thing. Keep it smaller than you think it should be. No guilt, no grand vows. If you pray, you can offer your three lines to God. If you don't, just keep them somewhere you'll see them. The bell holds the time.
Rule of life. From regula, a straight stick. A short, honest plan, daily, weekly, yearly, that holds the practices together.
Your line: small rules keep big loves. Today, finish your three lines and put them where you'll see them tomorrow. Camp three is done. Day one hundred fifty-six.

157.title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
157.hook: no birth story: Mark starts with a voice in the wilderness and a man in camel hair
157.carry: the beginning of the good news
157.howItsDone: In many churches, a passage from the Gospels is read aloud at every service, often with the congregation standing, and many Christians read through a gospel like Mark in order, a few verses a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a rule of life, and the close of camp three. Your line was small rules keep big loves. Are your three lines where you can see them? Now camp four: the text, read in order. Day one hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `SMALL RULES KEEP BIG LOVES.` → `CAMP FOUR: THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: If you know the Christmas story, you might expect a book about Jesus to start there: the manger, the shepherds, the star. Mark doesn't. Mark has no manger. No angels singing. No wise men. No baby at all. Mark skips all of it. It opens with one line, like a title, and then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild-looking man in camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, is shouting at crowds by a river. For the next several weeks, we're going to read Mark from the beginning, in order, a few verses at a time. Today, the very first word Mark uses for his book.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO ANGELS, NO BABY.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE.` → `A MAN IN CAMEL HAIR.`

segments.voice: Gospel. Here's how Mark begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Gospel is an Old English word, godspel, good news. It translates the Greek euangelion. And here's what first readers would have heard. In the Roman world, euangelion was the word for big public announcements: a victory in battle, a new emperor. An inscription from a city in what's now Turkey even calls the emperor Augustus's birthday the beginning of good news for the world. So when Mark calls his book the beginning of the good news of Jesus, it's a bold claim. The real good news, he's saying, is this. Then Mark quotes the prophets. "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." And there's the voice: John the Baptist. Mark gives us his outfit and his menu: "John was clothed with camel's hair, and with a girdle of a skin about his loins; and he did eat locusts and wild honey." That's not a random detail. The book of Kings remembers the prophet Elijah as a hairy man with a leather belt, and the prophet Malachi said Elijah would be sent before the great day of the Lord. Mark's readers would have noticed. Crowds come from all over Judea and Jerusalem to be baptized by John in the Jordan. But John points away from himself: "There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose." Eight verses, and Mark is already racing. That's his style. He doesn't linger. He wants you to feel that something is starting, right now. The beginning of the good news.
screen: `GODSPEL, EUANGELION — GOOD NEWS.` · `A WORD FOR EMPERORS' NEWS.` · `A VOICE IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `CAMEL HAIR, LIKE ELIJAH.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first eight verses of Mark aloud. If you have a Bible or an app nearby, open to Mark chapter one. If not, just hold the first line in your mind. Read slowly, out loud, even in a whisper. Notice how fast it moves: a title, a prophecy, a voice, a man in camel hair, crowds, a river, and then someone mightier coming. When you finish, sit with whichever image stayed with you. If you pray, you can offer it back. If you don't, just let it sit. The bell holds the time.
Gospel. From Old English for good news, translating the Greek euangelion, a word once used for an emperor's announcements.
Your line: the beginning of the good news. Today, read Mark chapter one, verses one to eight, out loud. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

158.title: The heavens torn open (Mark 1:9–13)
158.hook: the sky rips, the Spirit comes down like a dove, then straight into the desert
158.howItsDone: Many churches remember Jesus's baptism at the feast of the Baptism of the Lord or Theophany in January, and some lectionaries read Mark's desert verses at the start of Lent, when a season of forty days begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gospel, good news, and a man in camel hair by the Jordan. Your line was the beginning of the good news. Did you read those first eight verses aloud? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Yesterday John said someone mightier was coming. Today he arrives, and Mark gives him no introduction at all. No backstory. No childhood. Just: in those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. One sentence. He walks down into the river with everyone else. Then he comes up out of the water, and something happens that Mark describes with a word so violent it's almost shocking. Not the sky opening politely, like curtains. The sky ripping. And then, before you've even caught your breath, it's over, and he's alone in the desert. Five verses. Today: the heavens torn open.
screen: `NO BACKSTORY, ONE SENTENCE.` → `INTO THE RIVER WITH EVERYONE.` → `THE SKY RIPS.`

segments.voice: The heavens torn open. The King James Bible says it gently: "And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him." But the Greek word Mark uses is schizō: to tear, to split, to rip. It's where we get the word schism. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, use the ordinary word for open. Mark says torn. And the verb comes back at the very end of Mark: when Jesus dies on the cross, the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. The same word. Beginning and end. Mark is framing his whole story: heaven ripped open to earth. Then a voice: "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when this comes. Before a single miracle. Before a sermon. Before he's done anything at all. Beloved first. And then, right away, the turn. "And immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." Driveth. It's a strong word, the same one Mark later uses for casting out demons. The same Spirit that came down like a dove now drives him out. Forty days in the wilderness, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serving him. Mark gives none of the conversation with the tempter that Matthew and Luke tell. Just wild animals and angels, side by side. Some readers take comfort from the order: being beloved doesn't mean skipping the desert. Jesus heard the voice, and then went straight into the wilderness. In Mark, the voice comes first.
screen: `SCHIZŌ — THE SKY RIPS.` · `TORN AT THE START, TORN AT THE CROSS.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE'D DONE ANYTHING.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Notice how fast Mark moves: river, sky, dove, voice, desert, all in a few breaths. Now slow it down. Picture the water. Picture coming up out of it. If you're a Christian, you might hear the voice as spoken to you too, through baptism: beloved. If you're not, you can simply notice what it would mean to be loved before you've done anything. Then think about the desert you're walking into this week. Let the first word go with you into it. The bell holds the time.
The heavens torn open. Mark's word is schizō, to rip, and he uses it again when the Temple curtain tears at the cross.
Your line: beloved, then the desert. Today, when something hard comes, remember that the voice came before the wilderness. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: Follow me (Mark 1:14–20)
159.hook: Mark's favorite word: immediately they left their nets
159.howItsDone: Many Christians read the calling of the first disciples as a call to their own lives, and churches often read it when commissioning people for new work or ministry.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heavens torn open, a voice saying beloved, and then the desert. Your line was beloved, then the desert. Did the first word go with you? Day one hundred fifty-nine.

Early morning on the Sea of Galilee. It's really a lake, and the fishing is hard work: nets, boats, cold water, a family business. Two brothers, Simon and Andrew, are standing in the shallows casting a net. A man walks along the shore. He stops, looks at them, and says two words, more or less: follow me. And then Mark tells us what they did, and the word he uses is the heartbeat of his whole gospel. Down the beach, it happens again, with two more brothers, James and John, mending nets in their father's boat. The opposite of what they do is familiar: meant to, planned to, will get to it. Today's word is the one Mark keeps coming back to.
screen: `EARLY MORNING ON THE LAKE.` → `TWO BROTHERS CASTING A NET.` → `FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark uses it again and again; read him in one sitting and it's everywhere. The King James Bible often translates it straightway. Once you notice it, you can't stop: straightway he saw the heavens torn, immediately the Spirit drove him out, and now this. First, Mark sets the scene. John the Baptist has been arrested. Jesus comes into Galilee announcing: "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." Repent, in Mark's Greek, is about a change of mind, a new direction. And then the lake. He sees Simon and Andrew casting a net, and says: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to become fishers of men." A fisherman's joke, almost: you catch fish now, you'll catch people. And then: "And straightway they forsook their nets, and followed him." Straightway. Immediately. No negotiation, no three-month notice. A little further on, James and John are in their boat with their father, Zebedee. Jesus calls them, and they leave their father in the boat with the hired men, and go. Mark doesn't tell us what they were thinking. He doesn't say whether they'd met Jesus before; John's gospel suggests some of them had. He just shows the speed. Readers notice the cost, too: a father left sitting in a boat. For Mark, immediately is not recklessness. It's the rhythm of a story where God's time has arrived and can't wait. Some readers hear it as a question put to them: what's the net in my hands, and what would it mean to put it down?
screen: `EUTHYS — AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `THE TIME IS FULFILLED.` · `FISHERS OF MEN.` · `A FATHER LEFT IN THE BOAT.` · then, large: `STRAIGHTWAY THEY FORSOOK THEIR NETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing you've been putting off. Not a huge life change. Something small and kind or true. Texting a friend who's struggling. Apologizing. Signing up to help. Returning the call. Opening the Bible you meant to open. Notice the net in your hands: the reasons, the timing, the someday. For these two minutes, just picture putting it down and doing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it today. The bell holds the time.
Immediately. In Greek, euthys. Mark's word, again and again, the heartbeat of a story that won't wait.
Your line: leave the nets. Today, do one good thing immediately, the moment you think of it. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

160.title: Authority in Capernaum (Mark 1:21–28)
160.hook: in the synagogue he teaches with authority, and an unclean spirit shrieks
160.tomorrow: a mother-in-law and a whole town
160.howItsDone: Many Christians read Mark's healing and deliverance stories as signs of Jesus's authority over evil; churches differ in how they understand unclean spirits today, and many pray for freedom from whatever binds a person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: immediately, Mark's favorite word, and four fishermen dropping their nets. Your line was leave the nets. What did you do right away? Day one hundred sixty.

Saturday morning in a fishing town called Capernaum, on the north shore of the lake. It's the Sabbath, and the town is at the synagogue. A visiting teacher is invited to speak, which was normal. What isn't normal is how he speaks. People lean in. Something in his voice is different from anything they've heard. And then, in the middle of it, a scream. A man in the congregation, a man with what Mark calls an unclean spirit, shrieking at the teacher, as if something inside him knows exactly who this is and is terrified. Everyone freezes. Today: what happened next, and the word the whole town was talking about by lunchtime.
screen: `SABBATH IN CAPERNAUM.` → `THE WAY HE SPEAKS.` → `A SCREAM IN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Authority in Capernaum. First, the teaching. Mark says, in the King James Bible: "And they were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes." The scribes were careful teachers, and good ones often taught by citing earlier teachers: this rabbi said, that sage said. Jesus seems to speak directly. The Greek for authority is exousia. It comes from a verb that means it is allowed, it's in your power. So exousia is the right to act, and to say so. The scribes borrowed theirs from the teachers before them. Jesus speaks as if the right is his own, with no footnote. Mark never tells us what Jesus taught that morning. Just how it landed. Then the scream. "Let us alone; what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth? art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God." Here's the odd thing: in Mark, the spirits are the first to recognize who Jesus is, before the disciples, before the crowds. And Jesus doesn't want their announcement. "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." Hold thy peace is gentle in English. The Greek is blunt: be muzzled. Be quiet. Then: come out. The man convulses, the spirit cries out, and it's gone. And the town talks about one thing: what is this? A new teaching, with authority, and even the unclean spirits obey him. Christians read these stories in different ways. Many understand them as real encounters with spiritual evil. Many also hear in them every voice that holds a person captive and won't let go. Mark's point is the same either way: the same authority that teaches also frees. One word, and the man got his life back.
screen: `NOT AS THE SCRIBES.` · `EXOUSIA — THE RIGHT TO ACT.` · `THE SPIRITS KNOW HIM FIRST.` · `BE MUZZLED. COME OUT.` · then, large: `HOLD THY PEACE, AND COME OUT OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Most of us carry a voice inside that doesn't help. The one that says you're not enough, you'll fail, nobody wants you here. Listen for it gently. Don't argue with it. Just notice what it says and how old it sounds. If the voice is heavy or frightening, that's something to share with someone you trust or a professional, not to carry alone. If you pray, you can bring it to God and say the words of the story: be quiet, come out. If you don't, you can simply set it down for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Authority in Capernaum. Exousia: the right to act, spoken as his own. It teaches, and it frees.
Your line: be quiet, come out. Today, when a voice in you starts tearing you down, notice it, and don't let it run the room. Day one hundred sixty.

161.title: A mother-in-law and a whole town (Mark 1:29–39)
161.word: A mother-in-law and a whole town
161.hook: he heals Peter's mother-in-law, the whole town crowds the door, and before dawn he slips off to pray
161.howItsDone: Many Christians rise early to pray, following Jesus's example in Mark 1:35, and monastic communities keep prayers in the dark before dawn, often called vigils or matins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: authority in Capernaum, a scream in the synagogue, and two words, be quiet, come out. Your line was be quiet, come out. Did a hard inner voice lose the room? Day one hundred sixty-one.

Same Sabbath, a few hours later. They walk out of the synagogue, still buzzing, and go straight to Simon and Andrew's house for a meal. Yes, Simon, the one we call Peter, had a house, and a wife, and a mother-in-law. And she's in bed with a fever. The scene is so domestic it's almost funny: a crowded little house, a sick relative, guests arriving, nobody cooking. By sundown, the whole town will be at that door. And the next morning, before anyone is awake, Jesus will be gone. Today: one day in Capernaum, from a fever to the dark before dawn.
screen: `LUNCH AT SIMON'S HOUSE.` → `A MOTHER-IN-LAW WITH A FEVER.` → `BY SUNDOWN, THE WHOLE TOWN.`

segments.voice: A mother-in-law and a whole town. Mark tells it in three scenes. Scene one, the bedroom. They tell Jesus about her right away. In the King James Bible: "And he came and took her by the hand, and lifted her up; and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them." He takes her hand. Lifts her up. That word, raised, is the same word later used for resurrection. And then she serves them. Some readers wince, as if she's healed just to make lunch. But the word is diakoneō, the root of deacon, and it's the very word Mark uses for what Jesus came to do: not to be served, but to serve. In Mark, only the angels in the desert have done it before her. Scene two, sundown. The Sabbath ends when the sun sets, which may be why they wait: now they can carry their sick. "And all the city was gathered together at the door." Picture it: the whole town, in the dusk, at one little doorway. He heals many. Scene three, the dark. "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed." A great while before day. Mark piles up three Greek words to say very early, still night, extremely. And his friends, Simon leading, hunt him down: "All men seek for thee." Everyone's looking for you. And Jesus says, in effect, let's go somewhere else: "Let us go into the next towns, that I may preach there also: for therefore came I forth." He doesn't stay to become Capernaum's celebrity healer. The prayer in the dark seems to have told him where to go next. We met this rhythm a few weeks ago in Luke: he withdrew. Mark shows it on day one.
screen: `HE TOOK HER BY THE HAND.` · `ALL THE CITY AT THE DOOR.` · `A GREAT WHILE BEFORE DAY.` · `LET US GO INTO THE NEXT TOWNS.` · then, large: `AND THERE PRAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about tomorrow morning. Imagine waking just ten minutes earlier than usual, while the house is still dark and quiet, before the town is at your door. Picture where you'd sit. A chair, a window, the edge of the bed. Picture what you'd do: pray, if you pray, or simply sit and listen to the quiet. You don't need to decide anything big. Just let those ten minutes become real in your mind. Then, if it seems right, set the alarm. The bell holds the time.
A mother-in-law and a whole town. One day in Capernaum: a hand that lifts, a crowd at the door, and prayer in the dark.
